_comment: Editorial layer. This file deliberately contains NO coordinates. Every position on the map comes from OpenStreetMap; entries here are matched to OSM features by name at runtime and only add context. 'checked' is the date the practical information below was last verified against the linked sources.

essentials.title: Emergency: dial 911
essentials.body: One number for police, fire and ambulance. Calls are dispatched from the National Emergency Call Centre at Samoa Fire and Emergency Services headquarters in Apia. The single 911 number replaced the old separate service numbers in January 2018.

essentials.title: Time: UTC+13, all year
essentials.body: Samoa sits at UTC+13 and has not observed daylight saving since 2021, so there is no seasonal clock change. Samoa is west of the International Date Line — it shares a calendar date with New Zealand and Australia, and is a day ahead of American Samoa, 40 km away.

essentials.title: Money: Samoan tālā (WST)
essentials.body: Cash still rules outside the main hotels and supermarkets. Apia has the densest concentration of banks and ATMs in the country — turn on the Money layer to see them. Draw what you need before heading out to the villages or across to Savaiʻi. Tipping is not a Samoan custom.

essentials.title: Driving: keep left
essentials.body: Samoa switched from right-hand to left-hand traffic in September 2009 and is the only country in the Pacific to have made the change in modern times. Roughly 40 km/h through Apia and the villages, around 55 km/h on the open road. Visitors need their home licence plus a temporary Samoan permit, normally arranged by the rental agent. Watch for dogs, pigs and pedestrians on village roads at all hours.

essentials.title: Sundays and sā (evening prayer)
essentials.body: Sunday is genuinely quiet: most shops and many restaurants close, and church is the centre of the day. In villages, a bell or conch marks sā, the early-evening prayer curfew — if you are walking or driving through a village when it sounds, stop and wait the few minutes until it lifts. Dress modestly away from resorts, and cover up when passing through a village.

essentials.title: Entry: 90-day visitor permit on arrival
essentials.body: Citizens of most countries are issued a free 90-day Visitor's Permit on arrival, subject to holding a passport valid at least six months and an onward or return ticket. Extensions are lodged at the Immigration Office in Apia before the permit expires. Confirm your own nationality's position with an official source before travelling.

essentials.title: Buses: cash, and no timetable
essentials.body: Apia's wooden-bodied buses run from two terminals — beside Maketi Fou (Fugalei Market) and at Savalalo, behind the flea market off Mulinuʻu Road. There is no published timetable; buses leave when full and thin out sharply in the afternoon and barely run on Sunday. You pay the driver in cash as you get off, and fares around Apia are a few tālā.

sources.label: Samoa Tourism Authority — taking a bus

essentials.title: Airport: Faleolo (APW), west of town
essentials.body: Faleolo International is about 35 km west of Apia along the north coast — budget 45 to 60 minutes by road, more in morning traffic. Fagaliʻi Airfield, a few minutes east of the centre, has opened and closed repeatedly over the past decade; check its current status before assuming a flight uses it.

essentials.title: Savaiʻi ferry: Mulifanua – Salelologa
essentials.body: The inter-island ferry runs from Mulifanua wharf at the far west of Upolu, next to Faleolo, across to Salelologa on Savaiʻi. Sailings are operated by the Samoa Shipping Corporation and the crossing takes roughly an hour to ninety minutes. Vehicle space is limited and sailings change with weather and season — check the day before.

essentials.title: Wet season and cyclones
essentials.body: Samoa is tropical year round. The wetter, more humid season runs roughly November to April, which is also the South Pacific cyclone season; May to October is drier and slightly cooler. Heavy rain can flood the Vaisigano River and low-lying parts of central Apia within an hour.

notices.title: Savalalo bus terminal is being rebuilt
notices.body: Work to upgrade the Savalalo bus terminal began in February 2026, starting with the removal of the old shelters and the vendor stalls around the site. The government allocated around WST$3 million, and the intention is for the area to serve buses only, with vendors relocating to a new flea market facility. Expect bus stands, stalls and traffic around Savalalo and Mulinuʻu Road to differ from what is mapped.

notices.title: Apia waterfront redevelopment
notices.body: Beach Road and the harbour frontage are covered by the Apia Waterfront Plan 2017–2026, a staged programme of seawall, public space and road work along the central waterfront. Sections of the foreshore have been reshaped over the life of the plan, so mapped paths and frontages near Beach Road may be out of date.

sources.label: Waterfront Plan 2017–2026 (Ministry of Works, Transport & Infrastructure)

highlights.blurb: The house Robert Louis Stevenson built in 1890 and lived in until his death in 1894, restored as a museum. Samoans knew him as Tusitala, 'teller of tales'.
highlights.tip: The trail up Mount Vāea to his tomb starts near the museum grounds — steep, humid, and worth it for the view over Apia.

highlights.blurb: The Catholic cathedral on Beach Road and the defining silhouette of the Apia waterfront. The current building replaced the 19th-century cathedral on the same site and was reconsecrated in 2014.
highlights.tip: Visitors are welcome outside services. Cover shoulders and knees.

highlights.blurb: The Apia clock tower stands on the roundabout at the centre of the waterfront, built as a memorial to Samoans who served in the First World War. It is the landmark locals give directions from.
Apia's main produce market — taro, breadfruit, bananas, coconuts, kava and cooked food, under one big roof. Busiest and best early in the morning.
highlights.tip: One of the two main bus terminals sits alongside it.

highlights.blurb: The harbourside fish market, at its best not long after dawn when the boats come in — tuna, reef fish, octopus and oka (raw fish in coconut cream).
A marine reserve at the eastern end of the harbour where the reef flat drops away into a deep blue hole. The best snorkelling within walking distance of central Apia.
highlights.tip: Go at high tide — at low tide the walk out across the reef flat is shallow and sharp. Reef shoes help.

highlights.blurb: The national museum, housed in a former German colonial-era school building. Small, free or low cost, and a good grounding in faʻa Samoa, tattooing, navigation and the colonial period.
A living-culture demonstration on the waterfront — ʻava ceremony, siapo making, wood carving, coconut husking, umu (earth oven) cooking and dance, run by the Samoa Tourism Authority.
highlights.tip: Runs on set weekday sessions rather than continuously — check times before going.

highlights.blurb: The peninsula west of the centre holds Samoa's Parliament, the tombs of former heads of state and paramount chiefs, and the old Apia Observatory. It is the country's ceremonial and political ground.
highlights.tip: Quiet, open and good at sunset, but treat the tombs and grounds as the solemn places they are.

highlights.blurb: The national stadium and sports complex, home ground for Manu Samoa rugby and a venue for the 2019 Pacific Games.

The Bahá'í House of Worship at Tiapapata, in the hills south of Apia — one of only a small number of continental Bahá'í temples in the world, opened in 1984. Its nine-sided dome is visible from the cross-island road.
highlights.tip: Open to visitors of any faith; the gardens are the draw as much as the building.

highlights.blurb: Papaseʻea Sliding Rocks — a set of smooth waterfall chutes in the hills south of Apia that you slide down into freshwater pools.
highlights.tip: Water level makes or breaks it: thin in the dry months, and the steps down are slippery. A village entry fee applies.

highlights.blurb: The eastern side of the harbour — Vaiala Beach and the causeway out to Taumeasina island give the closest easy swimming to the town centre.
Samoa's national university, at Le Papaigalagala on the eastern edge of Apia.
Tupua Tamasese Meaole Hospital at Motoʻotua is the national referral hospital and the main emergency facility in the country.
highlights.tip: Serious cases are normally evacuated to New Zealand — travel insurance that covers aeromedical evacuation is strongly advised.

highlights.blurb: Samoa's international gateway (APW), about 35 km west of Apia on the north coast road.
highlights.tip: Allow a full hour from central Apia, and more if you are travelling during the morning school and work run.

highlights.blurb: The wharf at the western tip of Upolu where the Savaiʻi ferry departs, next door to Faleolo airport.

walks.title: Waterfront & markets loop
walks.blurb: The classic central Apia circuit: the clock tower, the cathedral, the national museum, then the harbourside fish market and the big produce market, finishing at Parliament on the Mulinuʻu peninsula.
walks.tip: Go in the morning — the markets are at their best before 10am and the waterfront has shade only early. Everything here is flat, easy walking.

stops.note: Start at the roundabout everyone in Apia gives directions from — the WWI memorial clock tower.
The white cathedral that defines the waterfront skyline. Visitors welcome outside mass; cover shoulders and knees.
Small, cheap, and the best half-hour grounding in faʻa Samoa you will get.
Best just after dawn when the boats come in. Try oka — raw fish in coconut cream.
The main produce market: taro, breadfruit, kava, cooked food. Locals call it Maketi Fou.
Finish on the ceremonial peninsula: Parliament, the tombs of paramount chiefs, and a good sunset.

walks.title: Vailima & the hills
walks.blurb: The sights in the hills behind Apia, best strung together by car or taxi: Robert Louis Stevenson’s house, the Baháʼí temple on the cross-island road, and the Papaseʻea sliding rocks.
walks.tip: Do Vailima first and climb Mount Vāea early, before the heat. The temple gardens are a cool stop afterwards; the sliding rocks need decent water flow, so ask locally in the dry season.

stops.note: Stevenson’s restored house. The trail to his tomb on Mount Vāea starts by the grounds — steep, 30–60 minutes.
One of the world’s few continental Baháʼí Houses of Worship, open to all. The gardens are the highlight.
Natural waterslides into freshwater pools. Village entry fee; slippery steps down.

walks.title: East harbour & Palolo Deep
walks.blurb: The quieter east side of the harbour: out along the shore to the Palolo Deep marine reserve — the best snorkelling within walking distance of town — and on to the Taumeasina causeway.
walks.tip: Palolo Deep is only worth it at high tide; at low tide the reef flat walk is shallow and sharp. Reef shoes strongly advised.

stops.note: A blue hole in the reef flat. Snorkel gear rentable at the entrance; small entry fee.
The Taumeasina side — the closest easy swimming to the town centre.
